newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Liberian leader tells child soldiers to go home.
newsitem.headline: Liberian leader tells child soldiers to go home.

text.p: Liberia's temporary head of state Ruth Perry made an impassioned plea on Thursday for child soldiers in her country's civil war to return home.
Perry, the first African woman to head a modern state, told reporters in neighbouring Ivory Coast she was travelling to the United Nations to drum up support for her appeal.
"It's about time child soldiers got out of the bush and came back home," Perry said during a stop in Abidjan.
Perry held up a fresh palm frond and a white handkerchief to reporters to symbolise her peace gesture to child soldiers swelling the ranks of Liberia's ethnic militias.

"Before I left I proceeded on a peace campaign with an olive branch and a white handkerchief. I asked all the other women to join me in appealing to all those people causing the war to come back home," Perry said.
Describing her job as a challenge to womanhood, Perry added: "I would like to ask women all over the world to help me push this process through to bring peace to Liberia."
She said she would appeal at the U.N. for international aid to help end the war, reintegrate the 60,000 guerrillas including child soldiers, and return Liberia to democratic rule.
Perry was appointed in August at a summit of West African heads of state trying to end the conflict in Liberia.
Warlords who reneged on more than a dozen previous peace accords pledged at the summit to disarm their guerrillas and implement a peace process leading to elections next May.
But despite symbolic gestures of dimobilisation, violence erupted in the last two weeks in western Liberia, and guerrillas prevented international aid reaching starving people.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Wednesday expressed shock at reports of weekend massacres in Grand Cape Mount County, where thousands have been cut off from relief aid.

U.N. reports said a "cold-blooded massacre" took place at Sinje on Saturday, leaving at least 17 civilians dead, many more wounded, and forcing about 1,000 others to flee the area. Some reports put the number dead at 42.
